planting.note: Install container plants in spring in rocky, fast-draining soil in full sun; the shimmering silver foliage needs reflected heat and lean conditions to perform, so avoid rich or regularly irrigated garden beds.

directions: Set plants in full sun and gritty, sharply drained soil, since this Texas sage dislikes humidity and wet feet far more than it dislikes heat. Silvery gray-green leaves hold up through extreme heat and extended dry spells once established, and lavender-purple flowers appear in flushes from summer into fall, often triggered by changes in humidity. Trim lightly in late winter or early spring to keep the naturally rounded form dense, and remove spent flower clusters if a tidier look is wanted. The plant is notably deer-, salt-, and drought-tolerant, making it a good fit for xeric borders, hedges, or mass plantings in hot, dry climates.
sources: Garden Debut (gardendebut.com) - Desperado Sage product page

planting.note: Plant balled or container specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in sun to partial shade; the strongly weeping, pendulous branch tips need an open spot or raised position where the cascading habit can be seen rather than crowded by other plants.

directions: Site this slow-growing weeper in sun to partial shade and evenly moist, well-drained soil, since Japanese maple roots are shallow and sensitive to drought stress and waterlogging alike. New foliage emerges a vivid crimson red, matures to burgundy through summer, and shifts to rusty red tones in fall, giving the strongly horizontal, cascading branch structure three seasons of color. Keep a steady layer of mulch over the root zone, water deeply during dry spells, and feed in early spring and again in early fall with an all-purpose fertilizer. Shelter the tree from harsh winds and heavy snow load, and keep lawn equipment well away from the trunk to avoid bark wounds on this ornamental specimen tree.

planting.note: Plant container or balled trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun, siting where the narrow, columnar form fits tight spaces such as street strips or courtyards without crowding structures.

directions: Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, digging a hole roughly one and a half times wider than the root ball and keeping the crown at grade. This selection is a dense, slow-growing, male clone, so it never produces the malodorous fruit associated with female ginkgo trees, while still turning a clean golden yellow in fall after rich green summer foliage. Water new plantings frequently until established, then taper off as the tree settles in, and apply an all-purpose fertilizer in early spring and fall. The tight, upright column habit makes this one of the better ginkgo choices for narrow urban or courtyard planting sites where a wide-spreading tree would not fit.
sources: Garden Debut (gardendebut.com) - Sky Tower Ginkgo product page

planting.note: Plant balled or container trees in spring or fall in consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in sun to partial shade; afternoon shade helps the deep red bracts and burgundy fall foliage hold their color in hot climates.

directions: This native flowering dogwood selection opens exceptionally deep red flower bracts in spring, a notable departure from the pink or white tones of most dogwoods, followed by red-tinted new growth and a rich burgundy fall color. Grow it in moderate, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist, avoiding both drought stress and standing water, which dogwood roots tolerate poorly. Prune only in late winter or early spring, since cuts made in late fall or winter are more prone to bark splitting and dieback on this species. Mulch over the root zone to conserve moisture and keep string trimmers away from the trunk, and give the tree afternoon shade where summers run hot to protect its deep color from fading.

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring near a sturdy trellis, arbor, or pergola in full sun and well-drained soil; strong permanent support is essential before growth takes off, since this vine quickly becomes heavy and woody.

directions: Install this reblooming Japanese wisteria against a sturdy arbor, pergola, or trellis in full sun and well-drained soil kept evenly moist but never waterlogged. Large, fragrant lavender flower clusters open before the foliage in spring, and unlike many wisterias, this selection produces additional flushes of bloom later in the growing season rather than flowering only once. Because the vine grows vigorously and can become invasive without control, cut back lateral shoots to about six inches from the main framework in summer and remove dead or damaged wood in winter to keep it within bounds. Feed with a balanced fertilizer in spring and summer, and train young growth onto permanent supports early, since mature wisteria vines are too heavy for flimsy structures.

planting.note: Plant balled or container trees in spring or fall in full sun; this selection was chosen for a stronger, more attractive branching structure while young than seedling black gum typically shows.

directions: Plant this native black gum selection in full sun, where it develops a notably strong, attractive branching habit from an early age compared to typical seedling-grown trees. Glossy medium-green summer foliage turns fiery red in fall, and the species' natural tolerance for both flooding and drought makes it adaptable to a wide range of soils and sites. Water deeply and regularly while the tree establishes, then rely on its native toughness once roots are developed, mulching the base to retain moisture. Prune in late winter or early spring to remove any crossing or damaged limbs, since black gum resents heavy pruning once mature.

planting.note: Plant balled or container trees in spring or fall in full sun as a shade or specimen tree; large glossy red new growth in spring is the standout feature that sets this black gum selection apart.

directions: This black gum selection opens large glossy red new leaves in spring that mature to glossy green through summer before red tones return in fall, giving it an extra flush of color beyond the species' usual single fall display. Grow in full sun and deep, evenly moist but not soggy soil, since black gum develops a long taproot that resents transplanting once established. Feed with a balanced 10-10-10 fertilizer in early spring and midsummer, mulch around the base to conserve moisture and suppress weeds, and limit pruning to late winter or early spring. Once rooted in, this slow-growing selection tolerates drought well and makes a durable long-term shade tree.

planting.note: Plant balled or container trees in spring or fall in full sun; black gum tolerates an unusually wide range of moisture extremes, from periodic flooding to dry upland sites, so siting is flexible.

directions: Bright red new growth opens in spring on this native black gum selection, settling into dark green through the summer before the foliage turns fiery red again in fall. It is notably adaptable, tolerating sites ranging from swampy, flood-prone ground to dry ridges and uplands, which makes it a forgiving shade tree choice across variable landscapes. Water regularly and deeply while young so the soil stays moist without becoming saturated, and feed in early spring and midsummer with a balanced 10-10-10 fertilizer. Prune in late winter or early spring only as needed to remove damaged wood, and mulch the root zone to conserve moisture on drier sites.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; the upright, arching form works well as a flowering screen or informal hedge where late-season fragrant bloom is wanted.

directions: Site this multi-season shrub in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil of average fertility, where clusters of fragrant, creamy-white flowers can open in late summer when few other woody plants are still blooming. After bloom, the flowers give way to showy red calyxes that provide a second round of color into fall, followed by yellow fall foliage and exfoliating bark for winter interest. Prune in early spring to control size and remove any crossing or damaged stems, since flowers form on the current season's growth. Established plants are deer-resistant and tolerate average garden conditions with only moderate watering, making the dense, arching habit useful for informal screening or privacy hedging.

planting.note: Plant balled or container trees in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; the compact pyramidal habit fits small-space gardens and privacy screening better than standard Cryptomeria.

directions: Grow this compact Japanese cedar in full sun to part shade and consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil, where its broad pyramidal form stays naturally dense without heavy shearing. Blue-green needle foliage resists the bronzing that often dulls Cryptomeria color in winter, keeping the tree attractive through the cold months, and it rarely sets the brown cones that detract from the look of larger relatives. Water during establishment and through dry spells, since shallow-rooted conifers can suffer in prolonged drought, and avoid heavy clay or poorly drained sites. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or damaged growth, making this a low-maintenance choice for a small-garden specimen or informal screen.
sources: First Editions (Bailey Nurseries) (firsteditionsplants.com) - Chapel View Japanese Cedar product page

planting.note: Plant balled or container trees in spring in full sun as a fast-growing shade or street tree; strong resistance to Dutch elm disease makes this selection a practical alternative to susceptible seedling American elms.

directions: This American elm selection was cloned from a mature tree that survived decades in a stand heavily infected with Dutch elm disease, giving it strong natural resistance that sets it apart from ordinary seedling elms. It grows quickly into the classic vase-shaped, broadly spreading canopy associated with American elm, with dark green summer foliage that turns yellow in fall. Plant in full sun and water regularly while the tree establishes its root system, then taper off once it is settled in, since mature elms tolerate average garden moisture well. Because its ultimate size is large, reserve this tree for open yards, parks, or street plantings with enough room for the wide, arching crown.
sources: First Editions (Bailey Nurseries) (firsteditionsplants.com) - St. Croix American Elm product page

planting.note: Plant balled or container trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; unlike the species, this selection flowers heavily every year rather than biennially, and starts blooming at a younger age.

directions: Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, where this Japanese tree lilac selection produces exceptionally heavy, fragrant, creamy-white flower clusters in June on branching that develops an attractive shelved, tiered look over time. Unlike seedling Japanese tree lilac, which often blooms only every other year, this selection flowers reliably every season and begins flowering at a younger age, and its larger, darker, glossier leaves resist common pests and diseases better than the species. Because the tree is sterile and sets no seedheads, cleanup stays minimal and there is no unwanted seedling spread. Prune only lightly after flowering to maintain shape, since this cultivar naturally grows about as wide as it is tall and needs little size correction.
